claim: Four 3D-EM datasets were acquired from mouse somatosensory (S1), secondary visual (V2), posterior parietal (PPC) and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC).
source: We acquired four 3D-EM datasets from mouse somatosensory (S1), secondary visual (V2), posterior parietal (PPC) and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) sized between 72 × 93 × 141 µm3 and 66 × 89 × 202 µm3 (Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Table 1 in Supplementary file 1) at a voxel size of 11.24–12 × 11.24–12 x 28–30 nm3 using serial block-face electron microscopy (SBEM [Denk and Horstmann, 2004]).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the acquisition of four datasets from specific brain regions with detailed dimensions and voxel sizes.

claim: The image volumes were located at the border of layers 1 and 2, the site of the main bifurcation of apical dendrites from almost all pyramidal neurons of layers 2 to 5.
source: The image volumes were located at the border of layers 1 and 2, the site of the main bifurcation of apical dendrites from almost all pyramidal neurons of layers 2 to 5 (Figure 1a,b).
evidence: The manuscript states the location of image volumes and references Figure 1a,b showing this anatomical positioning.

claim: 80–90% of all cortical pyramidal cells extend their apical dendrites into the L1/2 border region.
source: Since almost all pyramidal cells from cortical layers 2, 3 and 5 (and some from layer 4) form their apical dendrite's main bifurcation in this region, the layer 1/2 border in the upper cortex allows for synaptic convergence onto 80–90% of all cortical pyramidal cells (Larkman and Mason, 1990; Ito et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Larkman and Mason, 1990; Ito et al., 1998).

claim: The density of shaft synapses on DL ADs was 0.22 ± 0.02 synapses per µm dendritic shaft path length.
source: The density of shaft synapses on DL ADs was 0.22 ± 0.02 synapses per µm dendritic shaft path length (mean ± SEM, n = 41, Figure 1d,e).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative measurements with statistical parameters and references Figure 1d,e.

claim: DL ADs receive 2.16 ± 0.16 synapses onto spines per µm dendritic shaft path length.
source: Together with the substantial synaptic input to the spines of these ADs (Figure 1d,e, 2.16 ± 0.16 synapses onto spines per µm dendritic shaft path length), this yielded a fraction of 9.9 ± 5.1% (Figure 1f,g, mean ± SD, n = 41) shaft synapses at the main bifurcations of DL ADs in S1, V2, PPC and ACC cortex.
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative measurements with statistical parameters and references figures.

claim: DL ADs have a shaft synapse fraction of 9.9 ± 5.1% at their main bifurcations.
source: Together with the substantial synaptic input to the spines of these ADs (Figure 1d,e, 2.16 ± 0.16 synapses onto spines per µm dendritic shaft path length), this yielded a fraction of 9.9 ± 5.1% (Figure 1f,g, mean ± SD, n = 41) shaft synapses at the main bifurcations of DL ADs in S1, V2, PPC and ACC cortex.
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative measurements with statistical parameters and references figures.

claim: L2 ADs receive 0.42 ± 0.02 synapses per µm dendritic shaft path length at their shafts.
source: Here, unlike for DL ADs, we found substantial synaptic input to the shafts of the AD at the main bifurcation (Figure 1d,e, 0.42 ± 0.02 synapses per µm dendritic shaft path length, mean ± SEM, n = 41), with a fraction of 33.6 ± 17.9% (Figure 1f,g, mean ± SD, n = 41) of shaft synapses for S1, V2, PPC and ACC.
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative measurements with statistical parameters and references figures.

claim: L2 ADs have a shaft synapse fraction of 33.6 ± 17.9% at their main bifurcations.
source: Here, unlike for DL ADs, we found substantial synaptic input to the shafts of the AD at the main bifurcation (Figure 1d,e, 0.42 ± 0.02 synapses per µm dendritic shaft path length, mean ± SEM, n = 41), with a fraction of 33.6 ± 17.9% (Figure 1f,g, mean ± SD, n = 41) of shaft synapses for S1, V2, PPC and ACC.
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative measurements with statistical parameters and references figures.

claim: L2 ADs receive about 3-fold more relative synaptic input at the shafts of their main bifurcation compared to L3 and L5 pyramidal cells.
source: Thus, L2 ADs receive about 3-fold more relative synaptic input at the shafts of their main bifurcation compared to L3 and L5 pyramidal cells (9.9% vs 33.6%, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p < 10−11).
evidence: The manuscript provides a direct comparison with statistical testing showing significant difference.

claim: 91 of 92 axons seeded from the shafts of L2 ADs made at least 80% of their other output synapses onto shafts.
source: We found that, in fact, the preference of axons to either innervate shafts or spines of ADs was almost binary (Figure 2b): 91 of 92 axons seeded from the shafts of L2 ADs made at least 80% of their other output synapses again onto shafts (and 89 of 92 axons made at least 90% of their other synapses again onto shafts).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data on axonal targeting preferences with specific counts.

claim: 89 of 92 axons seeded from the shafts of L2 ADs made at least 90% of their other synapses onto shafts.
source: We found that, in fact, the preference of axons to either innervate shafts or spines of ADs was almost binary (Figure 2b): 91 of 92 axons seeded from the shafts of L2 ADs made at least 80% of their other output synapses again onto shafts (and 89 of 92 axons made at least 90% of their other synapses again onto shafts).

claim: 34 of 35 axons seeded from spines at L2 ADs made at least 80% of their other synapses as primary spine innervations.

claim: The clear dichotomy in axonal targeting supports the identification of spine-preferring axons as putative excitatory and shaft-preferring as putative inhibitory.

evidence: The claim is based on observed data patterns and supported by citation to Motta et al., 2019.

claim: The prediction accuracy of single synapses to predict the shaft or spine preference of the presynaptic axon was above 75% for most innervations, with most above 90%.

claim: Synapse size onto spines was indistinguishable between L2 and DL ADs.

claim: L2 ADs are 21% wider than DL ADs at their main bifurcation.

claim: There is a strong distance-dependence between the fraction of putative inhibitory synapses at the main bifurcation and the distance of the main bifurcation to the soma.

claim: The distance-dependence of putative inhibitory input fraction was weaker for the absolute density of excitatory or putative inhibitory synapses compared to their ratios.

evidence: The manuscript provides comparison of correlation strengths with R2 values.

source: We acquired four 3D-EM datasets from mouse somatosensory (S1), secondary visual (V2), posterior parietal (PPC) and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) sized between 72 × 93 × 141 µm3 and 66 × 89 × 202 µm3 (Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Table 1 in Supplementary file 1) at a voxel size of 11.24–12 × 11.24–12 x 28–30 nm3 using serial block-face electron microscopy (SBEM [Denk and Horstmann, 2004]).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the voxel size specifications.

claim: Synapses were identified based on the presence of vesicle cloud and postsynaptic density without consideration of the symmetry of pre- and postsynaptic densities.
source: Synapses onto ADs were identified as targeting the shafts vs. the spines of ADs (for an identification of shaft-preferring axons as putative inhibitory vs. spine-preferring axons as putative excitatory, see below) without consideration of the symmetry of pre- and postsynaptic densities (Gray, 1959; Colonnier, 1968).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the synapse identification method.

claim: In physiological experiments, evidence for a strong effect of GABA on regenerative activity in apical dendrites of thick-tufted L5 cells via non-synaptic GABA-B receptors had been reported.
source: In physiological experiments, evidence for a strong effect of GABA on regenerative activity in apical dendrites of thick-tufted L5 cells via non-synaptic GABA-B receptors had been reported (Pérez-Garci et al., 2006; Oláh et al., 2009; Pérez-Garci et al., 2013; Abs et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Previous studies in hippocampal pyramidal cells had reported a substantial increase in inhibitory synapse fraction towards the distal tuft dendrites which is driven mainly by a drop in excitatory synapse density.
source: Previous studies in hippocampal pyramidal cells had reported a substantial increase in inhibitory synapse fraction towards the distal tuft dendrites which is driven mainly by a drop in excitatory synapse density (Bannister and Larkman, 1995; Megías et al., 2001; Bloss et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: L5 pyramidal cells in cortex exhibit a distal putative inhibitory input domain similar to hippocampal pyramidal cells.
source: We find that L5 pyramidal cells in cortex exhibit a similar distal putative inhibitory input domain.

claim: The distal inhibitory domain is absent in the distal tufts of L2 and L3 pyramidal neurons.
source: This distal inhibitory domain, however, is absent in the distal tufts of L2 and L3 pyramidal neurons.

claim: Recent work using intracellular Gephyrin tagging underestimated the rate of spines by about ~20% compared to complete 3D EM based sampling.
source: Recent work using intracellular Gephyrin tagging for the detection of inhibitory synapses and counting of spines for excitatory synapses in LM (Iascone et al., 2018) underestimated the rate of spines by about ~20% compared to our complete 3D EM based sampling, resulting in an overestimation of the inhibitory-to-excitatory input fraction for L3 pyramidal cells (see also [Chen et al., 2012]).
evidence: The manuscript compares their results to previous work with citations.

claim: L5tt pyramidal cells may be controlled by overall and slow inhibition at their main bifurcations, but specific synaptic innervation at their distal dendrites.
source: Together with our evidence on low rates of synaptic putative inhibitory innervation at the main bifurcation of these pyramidal cells, this may indicate that L5tt pyramidal cells are controlled by overall and slow inhibition at their main bifurcations, but specific synaptic innervation at their distal dendrites, while L2 pyramidal cells receive specific synaptic inhibition at their main AD bifurcations.
evidence: The manuscript infers this mechanism based on combining their data with previous physiological findings.

claim: L2 pyramidal cells receive specific synaptic inhibition at their main AD bifurcations.
source: Together with our evidence on low rates of synaptic putative inhibitory innervation at the main bifurcation of these pyramidal cells, this may indicate that L5tt pyramidal cells are controlled by overall and slow inhibition at their main bifurcations, but specific synaptic innervation at their distal dendrites, while L2 pyramidal cells receive specific synaptic inhibition at their main AD bifurcations.
evidence: The manuscript infers this mechanism based on their data.

claim: The distinct putative inhibitory input profile of L3 pyramidal cells towards the tips of the apical dendrites may suggest that they allow for specific computations not shared by L2 or L5 pyramidal cells.
source: Their distinct putative inhibitory input profile towards the tips of the apical dendrites may suggest that they allow for specific computations not shared by L2 or L5 pyramidal cells.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about computational implications based on their findings.

claim: The findings imply unique innervation patterns for the apical dendrites of L2 vs L3 vs L5 pyramidal cells.
source: In conclusion, our findings describe non-random connectivity at the apical tuft input domain of pyramidal neurons in cortex. They imply unique innervation patterns for the apical dendrites of L2 vs L3 vs L5 pyramidal cells yielding highly variable and cell-type specific putative inhibitory-to-excitatory synaptic input compositions, and suggest differential modes of inhibitory operation for the main classes of pyramidal cells in the cortex.
evidence: The conclusion explicitly states this implication based on the findings.
